result: Post-translational modification of pili by glycosylation fine-tunes the rupture forces between pili. Wild-type pili show rupture forces of 39±1 pN, glycosylation-deficient (G−) pili show higher forces (46±1 pN for G−/G− interactions), and heterotypic interactions show lower forces (25±1 pN for G−/wt). The frequency of pilus retractions was not significantly different between strains.
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 provide quantitative force measurements from optical tweezers experiments (Figure 1B) showing differential rupture forces based on glycosylation status. Claim C56 provides a critical control showing retraction frequency is unchanged, confirming that force differences are due to altered pilus-pilus interactions rather than retraction dynamics. The measurements are internally consistent and support the conclusion in C58.

result: Engineered strains with varying pilus densities were created: P− (no pili), P++ (hyperpiliated with three pilE copies), and wild-type. The P++ strain is expected to have higher total attractive force due to increased pilus density, though individual pilus rupture forces should be unchanged.
evaluation: Claims C46-C47 describe the genetic construction and phenotypes of strains with altered pilus density, supported by strain construction details and citations. Claims C48-C49 are logical inferences based on the unchanged pilin sequence in P++ (thus unchanged individual pilus forces) but increased pilus number (thus increased total force). These are reasonable predictions that set up subsequent experiments.

result: In expanding colonies on agar plates, bacteria with lower pilus density (P−) segregate to the colony front. P− bacteria within 3 μm of the front show >50% probability of moving toward the front, compared to 50% for P+ controls. Similarly, P+ cells segregate to the front when mixed with hyperpiliated P++ cells. Sorting efficiency is highest near the expanding front.
evaluation: Claims C64-C69 describe quantitative observations from time-lapse microscopy (Figures 3-4) showing position-dependent segregation of less-piliated cells to the colony front. The probability analysis (C68-C69) provides statistical support. Claims C78-C79 appropriately summarize these findings. The spatial dependence of sorting efficiency is well-documented.

result: Pilus density affects bacterial generation time: P+ green (49±3 min), P− green (41±1 min), and P++ red (56±4 min). Despite faster growth of P− cells, their increased spatial variance as a function of offspring number indicates increased mobility within colonies. Control experiments with PQ− (similar generation time to P+) confirm that segregation is independent of growth rate differences.
evaluation: Claims C70-C72 provide generation time measurements (Table 2) showing pilus density inversely correlates with growth rate. Claim C73 presents variance analysis (Figure 5D) demonstrating increased P− mobility after accounting for growth differences. Claim C77 describes a critical control (PQ− strain) that decouples piliation from growth rate, confirming segregation is not simply due to faster growth. The analysis appropriately addresses a major confounding variable.

result: Bacteria with glycosylated pili (wild-type) segregate to the front of expanding colonies of glycosylation-deficient (G−) bacteria. The G− strain has a comparable generation time (50±2 min) to wild-type, indicating that sorting is due to differences in pilus-pilus rupture forces rather than growth rate differences.
evaluation: Claims C80-C83 describe experiments (Figure 6) showing segregation based on glycosylation status with matched generation times, eliminating growth rate as a confounding factor. Claim C84 appropriately infers that the differential rupture forces measured earlier (C53-C57) are the likely mechanism. The experimental design directly tests the role of post-translational modification in sorting.

result: In liquid culture, bacteria sort into distinct morphologies based on pilus density and glycosylation: P+/P+ form mixed spheres, P+/P− show no interaction, P++/P+ form core-shell structures, and P+/G− form partial engulfment (crescents). These morphologies correlate with measured rupture forces and match predictions of the differential adhesion hypothesis.
evaluation: Claims C86-C90 describe confocal microscopy observations (Figure 7, Videos 4-7) of distinct morphologies for different strain combinations. Claim C91 notes agreement with DAH predictions, and C92-C93 appropriately conclude that sorting depends on pilus properties and correlates with rupture forces. The four morphotypes provide systematic evidence linking physical forces to spatial organization.

result: Active force generation by T4P retraction is required for defined cluster morphologies. pilT deletion mutants (T−) that cannot retract pili form irregular, non-spherical clusters without sorting, even when glycosylation is varied. This demonstrates that passive adhesion alone is insufficient for the observed morphologies.
evaluation: Claims C94-C96 establish the pilT mutant phenotype (inability to retract pili/generate force) based on prior work. Claims C97-C99 describe experimental observations (Figure 8) showing loss of defined morphologies in T− strains. Claims C100 and C102 appropriately conclude that active force generation is necessary. This is a critical experiment distinguishing between passive (DAH) and active (DSAH) mechanisms.

result: The observed morphotypes in liquid culture are in remarkable agreement with predictions of the differential strength of adhesion hypothesis (DSAH). Each strain combination produces morphologies consistent with the relative rupture forces: equal forces yield mixing, zero forces yield no interaction, and intermediate force hierarchies yield core-shell or partial engulfment structures.
evaluation: Claims C105-C109 systematically relate each observed morphology to the measured force relationships, showing internal consistency between force measurements and spatial organization. Claims C5, C101, and C110 conclude agreement with DSAH predictions. The requirement for active force generation (previous result) supports DSAH over passive DAH. The comprehensive matching of predictions to observations across multiple strain combinations provides strong support.

result: Bacterial sorting in early biofilms is governed by differential physical interactions determined by pilus density and post-translational modification. Mechanical forces control cell sorting based on similar physical principles as in developing embryos, though the bacterial system involves only attractive forces from pilus retraction rather than the balance of adhesion and cortical contractility seen in eukaryotes.
evaluation: These claims represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from force measurements, agar plate sorting, liquid culture morphologies, and pilT mutant experiments. The evidence collectively demonstrates that physical forces govern bacterial sorting. The comparison to embryonic development is appropriately qualified (C113) by noting differences in force types. The conclusions are well-supported by the experimental results.

result: In control experiments with isogenic P+ strains, little mixing occurs during range expansion on agar plates, with fluorescent transformants forming sectors. Mobility is primarily determined by steric interactions from cell division, with T4P-mediated motility limited to 1-3 bacterial diameters at the expanding front. Sorting is incomplete in the bulk of colonies.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 describe control experiments (Figure 2, Videos 1-2) establishing baseline behavior without differential pilus properties. The sector formation is consistent with range expansion theory (C60 cites Hallatschek et al., 2007). Claim C66 appropriately notes that sorting is spatially restricted, which is important context for interpreting the main results. These controls are essential for validating the experimental system.

result: A pilQ deletion strain (PQ−) with slightly higher generation time than piliated controls still shows segregation to the colony front, confirming that pilus loss induces segregation independently of growth rate effects.
evaluation: Claims C74-C76 describe a control experiment (Figure 5—supplement 2) using a different genetic approach to eliminate pili while controlling for growth rate. This provides independent confirmation that segregation is due to pilus loss rather than growth rate differences, strengthening the conclusions about the role of physical interactions.

result: Bacteria likely employ a tug-of-war mechanism for segregation within microcolonies, similar to their surface motility. Unlike eukaryotic development where cortical contractility and adhesion act antagonistically, bacterial pilus retraction forces are always attractive, with the cell body acting as a point-object.
evaluation: Claim C103 cites prior work on tug-of-war motility. Claim C104 reasonably infers this mechanism operates in microcolonies based on the requirement for active force generation. Claim C113 appropriately distinguishes the bacterial system from eukaryotic development. These are reasonable mechanistic interpretations supported by the experimental evidence, though direct visualization of the tug-of-war in microcolonies is not provided.

result: Cell sorting based on pilus variation is likely biologically relevant for pathogenic Neisseria species, which naturally generate micro-heterogeneity through phase and antigenic variation of T4P-associated genes. The authors propose that this variation triggers cell sorting and affects biofilm architecture.
evaluation: Claims C115-C117 cite prior work establishing that Neisseria populations naturally vary pilus properties. Claims C114 and C118 propose biological relevance but are speculative (C114 explicitly uses "very likely" and C118 is labeled as speculation). While the proposal is reasonable given the experimental findings, direct evidence that natural variation causes sorting in vivo is not provided. This represents an important hypothesis for future work rather than a demonstrated result.

result: The introduction establishes the context by reviewing prior work on cell sorting in embryonic development (differential adhesion hypothesis, differential interfacial tension hypothesis, differential strength of adhesion hypothesis) and bacterial biofilms (T4P-mediated sorting in various species). The biophysical basis for bacterial sorting remains unclear despite observations in multiple systems.
evaluation: These claims summarize established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout. They provide necessary background for understanding the study's motivation and significance. The claims accurately represent prior work and identify the knowledge gap the study addresses. This is standard introductory material that contextualizes the research.

result: N. gonorrhoeae serves as an appropriate model system because gonococci are peritrichously piliated, T4P are necessary for microcolony formation, microcolonies show liquid-like behavior, T4P retraction generates mechanical force, and the bacteria are naturally competent for transformation. Wild-type gonococci have glycosylated pili, and deletion of pglF reduces glycosylation.
evaluation: These claims establish the properties of the model system, supported by citations to prior work (C40, C42-C45, C50-C52, C59) and established knowledge (C41). They justify the choice of N. gonorrhoeae as a model and provide necessary background on pilus biology and genetic manipulation. This information is essential for understanding the experimental approach.
